title: Microsoft Patches 1,094 Flaws, Including an Outlook Zero-Day Already Exploited
excerpt: November's Patch Tuesday fixes 1,094 Microsoft CVEs. The one to install first closes an Outlook spoofing flaw, already exploited, that can leak a user's NTLMv2 credential hash.
body:
• Microsoft's November 2026 security updates, released on Patch Tuesday, November 10, address 1,094 Microsoft CVEs — the second straight month above 1,000.
  • The urgent one: CVE-2026-124194, an Outlook spoofing flaw already exploited in the wild, can leak your NTLMv2 credential hash if you open a specially crafted message file.
  • CISA has added the Outlook flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog; US federal agencies must patch by November 24.
  • What to do: run Windows Update and update Outlook/Microsoft 365 now — the Preview Pane alone does not trigger this flaw, but opening the file does.

Microsoft has patched 1,094 vulnerabilities in its November 2026 security updates, and one of them is already being exploited: a spoofing flaw in Microsoft Outlook, tracked as CVE-2026-124194, that can hand an attacker your network credential hash. The updates were released on Patch Tuesday, November 10, and the company's own release notes put the count at 1,094 Microsoft CVEs, with a further 165 republished non-Microsoft CVEs included in the same release.

How the Outlook flaw works

According to Microsoft, an unauthenticated attacker can send a specially crafted message file and persuade a recipient to open it in an affected version of Outlook. Opening the file can make Outlook connect to an attacker-controlled network location without showing the usual warning about external content, and that connection can disclose the user's NTLMv2 authentication hash. The captured hash can then be used to try to impersonate the victim, authenticate to other services, or support offline password-cracking attempts. The flaw does not itself give an attacker code execution, and the Preview Pane alone does not trigger it — the file has to be opened. It affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and Office LTSC 2021 and 2024. Microsoft rates it moderate severity, with a CVSS score of 6.5 reported by SecurityWeek — a reminder that a moderate rating means little once exploitation is confirmed.

"Opening the file could cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual warning about external content."

— Microsoft, on CVE-2026-124194

What the 1,094 covers

Counted in Microsoft's total: flaws in Windows (726), Microsoft Office (174), SQL Server (59), developer tools (53), SharePoint (27), Azure (20), Exchange Server (9), Defender (1) and other products (25). SecurityWeek counts 66 of the flaws as critical. Two critical flaws carry CVSS scores of 9.8: CVE-2026-116928 in Windows Search, which is a particular concern in Exchange environments because attachments can be processed automatically for indexing, and CVE-2026-119958 in Windows LDAP, which could let an unauthenticated attacker run code remotely against vulnerable systems, including domain controllers. Totals published by different trackers vary — BleepingComputer's count of 1,235 includes Microsoft Edge (Chromium) flaws and a different scope — because the counters draw the boundaries differently; Microsoft's own figure for its own CVEs is 1,094. The release follows October's 1,411 flaws, which SecurityWeek described as record-breaking, and Microsoft has said it used AI tools to help find many of the defects.

What to do next

Install the November updates through Windows Update, and make sure Outlook and Microsoft 365 apps are updated rather than deferred — workplace machines managed by an IT department should get the fixes through the normal patch cycle, but the exploited Outlook flaw is the reason not to postpone. US federal civilian agencies are required to remediate CVE-2026-124194 by November 24 under CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and Japan's JPCERT/CC has also issued an alert urging organisations to apply the updates. Full details are in Microsoft's November 2026 release notes.
